card.title: IMPERIAL RESEARCH
card.text: Choose One - Add BALLOON BOMBS to hand OR add EXPANDED IMPERIAL R&D to hand.
card.flavorText: Imperial Japanese research during WWII produced weapons and materials that ranged from practical battlefield improvements to desperate late-war projects. One of the most effective was the Type 93 torpedo, later known as Long Lance. It used compressed oxygen instead of compressed air, which gave Japanese cruisers and destroyers’ torpedoes longer range, higher speed, and a smaller visible wake than many Allied torpedoes. Japanese engineers also helped push aircraft materials forward. Sumitomo developed Extra Super Duralumin, an aluminium alloy related to what later became 7075 aluminium. It was adopted for the Mitsubishi A6M Zero because it offered high strength with low weight, though it also required careful protection against corrosion. Other projects illustrated Japan’s search for unusual strategic weapons. Fu-Go balloon bombs used high altitude winds to cross the Pacific and carry incendiary and explosive payloads toward North America. About 9,300 were launched, but the campaign achieved little military effect. Imperial Weapon No. 2 referred to the Nakajima Kikka, Japan’s first turbojet-powered aircraft. It first flew in August 1945, but arrived too late for operational service.
